DifferentialEquation/CH2/exact-equations.title: exact equations
DifferentialEquation/CH2/exact-equations.content:
For a differential equation
M(x,y)d x + N(x,y)d y = 0
we will say it’s exact if and only if
(diff M)/(d y) = (diff N)/(d x)

DifferentialEquation/CH2/integrating-fac.title: integrating factor
DifferentialEquation/CH2/integrating-fac.content:
For
(d y)/(d t) + p(t) y(t) = g(t)
consider a mu(t) that
mu (d y)/(d t) + mu p(t) y(t) = mu g(t)
take (d mu)/(d t) = mu p(t) ==> mu = C e^(p(t) t)
therefore, we can turn the equation above to
d/(d t) (mu y) = mu g(t) ==> y = (integral mu g(t) d t + C)/mu
then plug \mu in as the solution.

DifferentialEquation/CH3/order-reduce-by.title: order reduce by substitution
DifferentialEquation/CH3/order-reduce-by.content:
a technique to solve higher order differential equation by setting additional variable to substitute. Then solve it by normal ODE method. Lastly substitute it back
Example
(2-t)u''' + (3-t)u'' = 0
where t < 2
consider z = u''
(2 - t) z' +(3 - t) z &= 0\
z' &= (t - 3)/(2 - t) z\
z' 1/z &= (t - 3)/(2 - t)\
z &= C e^(integral (t - 3)/(2 - t) d t)\
z &= C(t - 2) e^(-t)
then
u^('') &= C(t - 2) e^(-t) \
u' &= - C_1 e^(-t) (t - 1) + C_2 \
u &= - C_1 e^(-t) t + C_3 + C_2 t
square

where W is Wronskian determinant and c is a constant by W at convenient point.

DifferentialEquation/CH5/radius-of-conve.title: radius of convergence
DifferentialEquation/CH5/radius-of-conve.content:
for power series
sum_n^infinity a_n
like the content in Calculus II, do the ratio test
lim_(n -> infinity) | (a_(n + 1))/(a_n) |
then the radius of convergence is 1/N where N is at most what x can let it less than 1 (convergence condition).
Example
sum_(n = 0)^infinity 2^n x^n
So
a_n = 2^n x^n
and
a_(n + 1) = 2 x 2^n x^n
then
lim_(n -> infinity) | (a_(n + 1))/(a_n) | =|2 x|
Then we can say the radius of convergence is R = 1/N = 1/2.   square

DifferentialEquation/CH5/series-solution.title: series solutions
DifferentialEquation/CH5/series-solution.content:
consider
y = sum_(n = 0)^infinity a_n x^n
then
y' = sum_(n = 1)^infinity n a_n x^(n - 1) = sum_(n = 0)^infinity (n + 1) a_(n + 1) x^n
and
y^('') = sum_(n = 2)^infinity n(n - 1) a_n x^(n - 2) = sum_(n = 0)^infinity (n + 2)(n + 1) a_(n + 2) x^n
then solve the equation by normal calculation

DifferentialEquation/CH7/systems-of-firs.title: systems of first order ODEs
DifferentialEquation/CH7/systems-of-firs.content:
arrow(x)' = A arrow(x)
briefly we need to find all Eigenvectors:

find all Eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix A by solving det(A - lambda I)
for each lambda_i find (A - lambda_i I) arrow(xi)_i = arrow(0) where I is identify matrix and arrow(xi)_i is correspond Eigenvector
if the lambda_i is repeated eigenvalue (equivalent to repeated root), need to use (A - lambda_i I) arrow(xi)_(i + 1) = arrow(xi)_i to find the generalized eigenvector, this process also called Jordan Chain
lastly construct the homogeneous solution
 arrow(x)(t) = sum C_i xi_i e^(lambda_i t)

IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/algor.title: Dijkstra
IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/algor.content:
For shortest walk in weighted DAG.
Pseudo-code
#import "@preview/algo:0.3.6": algo, i, d, comment, code
#let sc(body) = {smallcaps(text(font:"")[#body])}

#algo(
  title: sc[Dijkstra],
  parameters: ("s",),
  fill: rgb(255, 255, 255, 20)
)[
  for all vertices $v in V$:#i\
  $v.d i s t <- infinity$\
  #d\
  $q <-$ priorityQueue($emptyset$)\
  $q.$#sc[Insert]$(s, 0)$\
  while $q$ is not empty:#i\
  $u <-$ #sc[ExtractMin]$(q)$ #comment[$O(log V)$]\
  for all edges $u -> v$:#i\
  if $u -> v$ is tense:#i\
  #sc[Relax]$(u -> v)$ #comment[update $v.d i s t$]\
  if $v in q$:#i\
  $q.$#sc[DecreaseKey]$(v, v.d i s t)$ #comment[$O(log V)$ or $O(1)$ if use Fibonacci heap] #d\
  else:#i\
  $q.$#sc[Insert]$(v, v.d i s t)$\
  #d#d#d#d\
]
Runtime
O((V + E) log V)
then if we use Fibonacci heap instead of binary heap in queue, it will be
O(V + E log V)
or worst cases(dense graph) O(V^2 log V)  and  O(V^2)

IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/algor.title: Tarjan
IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/algor.content:
To mark strong components.
Pseudo-code
#import "@preview/algo:0.3.6": algo, i, d, comment, code
#let sc(body) = {smallcaps(text(font:"")[#body])}

#algo(
  title: sc[TarjanDFS],
  parameters: ("v", "S", "E", "clock"),
  fill: rgb(255, 255, 255, 20)
)[
  #sc[Mark]$(v)$\
  $c l o c k <- c l o c k + 1$\
  $v.p r e <- c l o c k$\
  $v.l o w <- c l o c k$\
  $S.$#sc[Push]$(v)$\
  for all edges $v -> w in E$:#i\
  if $w$ is unmarked:#i\
  $c l o c k <-$ #sc[TarjanDFS]$(w, S, E, c l o c k)$\
  $v.l o w <-$ #sc[Min]$(v.l o w, w.l o w)$#d\
  else:#i\
  if $w.r o o t = "none"$:#i\
  $v.l o w <-$ #sc[Min]$(v.l o w, w.p r e)$\
  #d#d#d\
  if $v.l o w = v.p r e$:#i\
  do:#i\
  $w <- S.$#sc[Pop]$(space)$\
  $w.r o o t <- v$#d\
  while $w != v$\
  #d\
  return $c l o c k$\
]
\
#algo(
  title: sc[Tarjan],
  parameters: ("G",),
  fill: rgb(255, 255, 255, 20)
)[
  $c l o c k <- 0$\
  $S <-$ stack($emptyset$)\
  for all vertices $v in G.V$:#i\
  #sc[Unmark]$(v)$\
  $v.r o o t <- "none"$\
  #d\
  for all vertices $v$:#i\
  if $v$ is unmarked:#i\
  $c l o c k <-$ #sc[TarjanDFS]$(v, S, G.E, c l o c k)$\
  #d#d\
]

O(|V| + |E|)

IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/algor.title: Topological sort
IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/algor.content:
Note 1: it’s not possible to do topological order for non DAG graph
Note 2: there can be multiple topological order

Backward implementation by DFS pseudo-code
#import "@preview/algo:0.3.6": algo, i, d, comment, code
#let sc(body) = {smallcaps(text(font:"")[#body])}

#algo(
  title: sc[DFS],
  parameters: ("s", "clock", "S"),
  fill: rgb(255, 255, 255, 20)
)[
  $s.$state $<-$ active\
  for all edge $u -> v$:#i\
  if $v.$state $=$ new:#i\
  $c l o c k <-$ #sc[DFS]$(v, c l o c k)$#d\
  else:#i\
  if $v.$state $=$ active:#i\
  fail #comment[it should not has cycle because it should be DAG]\
  #d#d\
  $s.$state $<-$ finish\
  #d\
  $S[c l o c k] <- v$\
  $c l o c k <- c l o c k - 1$\
  return $c l o c k$\
]
\
#algo(
  title: sc[topologicalSort],
  parameters: ("s", "V"),
  fill: rgb(255, 255, 255, 20)
)[
  for all vertex $v in V$:#i\
  $v.$state $<-$ new\
  #d\
  $S <- emptyset$\
  $c l o c k <- |V|$\
  for all vertex $v in V$:#i\
  if $v.$state $=$ new:#i\
  $c l o c k <-$ #sc[DFS]$(v, c l o c k, S)$\
  #d#d\
  return $S[1 dots |V| ]$\
]

O(|V| + |E|)

IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/termi.title: terminologies
IntroToAlgs-and-ModelsOfComp/graph/termi.content:
Directed acrylic graph
known as DAG, a directed graph without any cycle.
Tense edge
If this edge can be improved the destination vertex shortest walk estimation
(forall u -> v) u . d i s t + w(u -> v) < v . d i s t
Relax edge operation
(forall u -> v) u -> v "is tense" ==> v . d i s t := u . d i s t + w(u -> v)
Negative cycle
Negative weight cycles make shortest paths undefined for any algorithm, as we can decrease cost infinitely by repeating the cycle.
Additionally, negative edge weights break Dijkstra’s greedy assumption.

NumericalAnalysis/CH2/Forward-backward-s.title: Forward-backward substitution
NumericalAnalysis/CH2/Forward-backward-s.content:
ref: ubcmath.github.io/MATH307/systems/lu.html#forward-and-backward-substitution

Given A=L U by LU factorization, we can adapt this technique to solve A x= b by L y=b and U x = y
Python code example for LU factorization
np.linalg
it is equivalent with codes:
y = np.linalg.solve(L, b)
x = np.linalg.solve(U, y)
custom implementation
import numpy as np
 
def fw_sub(L, b):
    n = L.shape[0]
    y = np.zeros((n, 1))
    
    for i in range(n):
        sum_val = 0
        for j in range(i):
            sum_val += L[i, j] * y[j, 0]
        y[i, 0] = (b[i, 0] - sum_val) / L[i, i]
    
    return y
 
def bw_sub(U, y):
    n = U.shape[0]
    x = np.zeros((n, 1))
    
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        sum_val = 0
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            sum_val += U[i, j] * x[j, 0]
        x[i, 0] = (y[i, 0] - sum_val) / U[i, i]
    
    return x
 
L = np.array([
	[1, 0, 0],
	[2, 1, 0],
	[1, 1, 1]
])
U = np.array([
	[2, 4, 2],
	[0, 1, 1],
	[0, 0, 1]
])
 
# solve Ax = b
A = L @ U
b = np.array([[-1], [1], [2]])
print(f"L={L}")
print(f"U={U}")
print(f"b={b}")
# A=[[2 4 2]
# [4 9 5]
# [2 5 4]]
print(f"A={A}")
 
# solve Ly = b
y = fw_sub(L, b)
# solve Ux = y
x = bw_sub(U, y)
 
# y=[[-1.]
#  [ 3.]
#  [ 0.]]
print(f"y={y}")
# x=[[-6.5]
#  [ 3. ]
#  [ 0. ]]
print(f"x={x}")
# Ax=[[-1.]
#  [ 1.]
#  [ 2.]]
# Ax should be eq to b
print(f"Ax={A @ x}")

import numpy as np
 
def LU(A):
	n = A.shape[0]
	U = A.copy()
	L = np.eye(n, dtype=np.double)
	for i in range(n):
		factor = U[i + 1:, i] / U[i, i]
		L[i + 1:, i] = factor
		U[i + 1:] -= factor[:, np.newaxis] * U[i]
	return L, U

import numpy as np
 
def lanczos_iter(A, tol=1e-8):
    n = A.shape[0]
    
    # q0 = np.zeros(n)  # q0 = 0
    # b0 = 0            # b0 = 0
    x0 = np.random.rand(n)
    q1 = x0 / np.linalg.norm(x0)
	
    Q = [q1]  # start with k = 1
    alphas = []
    betas = [b0]
	
    qk = q1
    qk_prev = q0
    bk_prev = b0
    
    for k in range(1, n+1):
        # u_k = A*q_k
        uk = A @ qk
		
		# .T same as .H cause it's real
        # a_k = q_k^T * u_k
        ak = qk.T @ uk
        alphas.append(ak)
        
        # u_k = u_k - b_{k-1}*q_{k-1} - a_k*q_k
        uk = uk - bk_prev * qk_prev - ak * qk
        
        # b_k = ||u_k||
        bk = np.linalg.norm(uk)
	    
        if abs(bk) < tol:
            break
            
        betas.append(bk)
        
        # q_{k+1} = u_k/b_k
        qk_next = uk / bk
        Q.append(qk_next)
        
	    
        qk_prev = qk
        qk = qk_next
        bk_prev = bk
    
    
    m = len(alphas)
    T = np.zeros((m, m))
    np.fill_diagonal(T, alphas)
    for i in range(m-1):
        T[i, i+1] = betas[i+1]
        T[i+1, i] = betas[i+1]
	    
    return np.column_stack(Q), T

import numpy as np
 
def arnoldi_iter(A, tol=1e-8):
    n = A.shape[0]
    x0 = np.random.rand(n)
    q1 = x0 / np.linalg.norm(x0)
    
    # Initialize properly
    Q = np.zeros((n, n+1))
    Q[:, 0] = q1
    H = np.zeros((n+1, n))
    
    for k in range(n):
        v = A @ Q[:, k]
        
        # Orthogonalization
        for j in range(k+1):
            H[j, k] = Q[:, j].T @ v
            v = v - H[j, k] * Q[:, j]
        
        H[k+1, k] = np.linalg.norm(v)
        
        if H[k+1, k] < tol:
            break
            
        Q[:, k+1] = v / H[k+1, k]
    
    return Q[:, :k+1], H[:k+2, :k+1]

import numpy as np
 
def rayleigh_quotient_iteration(A, num_iter, tol=1e-6):
	x_k = np.random.rand(A.shape[1])
	for _ in range(num_iter):
		sigma = x_k.T @ A @ x_k / (x_k.T @ x_k)
		y_k = np.linalg.solve(A - sigma * np.eye(A.shape[0]), x_k)
		x_k_o = x_k
		x_k = y_k / np.linalg.norm(y_k)
		if np.linalg.norm(x_k - x_k_o) < tol:
			break
	return x_k

def deflate_matrix(A, eigenvector, eigenvalue):

    v = eigenvector / np.linalg.norm(eigenvector)

NumericalAnalysis/CH6/multi/BFGS-Method.title: BFGS Method
NumericalAnalysis/CH6/multi/BFGS-Method.content:
Concept
BFGS Methodis a secant updating methods of quasi-Newton’s method.
take B_0 = I or initial guess of H.
solve B_k s_k = - nabla f(x_k)
x_{k + 1} = x_k + s_k
y_k = nabla f(x_(k + 1)) - nabla f(x_k)
B_(k + 1) = B_k + (y_k y_k^T)/(y_k^T s_k) - (B_k s_k s_k^T B_k)/(s_k^T B_k s_k)
repeat this.

NumericalAnalysis/CH6/multi/Conjugate-Gr.title: Conjugate Gradient Method
NumericalAnalysis/CH6/multi/Conjugate-Gr.content:
Concept
the first part is same as Steepest Descent Method, but after find the new x, we calculate next g instead of finding steepest descent by
beta = (g_1^T g_1)/(g_0^T g_0)
and
s_1 = - g_1 + beta s_0
x0 = initial guess
g0 = \nabla f(x0)
s0 = g0
for k = 0, 1, 2,...
	Choose αk to minimize f(xk + αk sk)
	xk+1 = xk + αk sk
	gk+1 = \nabla f(xk+1)
	βk+1 = (g^Tk+1 gk+1)/(g^Tk gk)
	sk+1 = gk+1 + βk+1sk
end

Conjugate Gradient Method is only different with Steepest Descent Method with beta, if we set beta constantly equal to 0, it will be same as Steepest Descent Method.
Cost
unlike Newton’s method, this one doesn’t need to calculate Hessian matrix H nor b, it only need to calculate gradient nabla and line search.

Code
import numpy as np
from typing import Callable, Tuple
 
def backtracking_line_search(  
	f: Callable[[np.ndarray], float],  
	grad_f: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray],  
	x: np.ndarray,  
	d: np.ndarray, # direction, usually - \nabla grad_f 
	alpha_init: float = 1.0,  
	rho: float = 0.5, # back trace factor  
	c: float = 1e-4 # Armijo cond 
) -> float:
	alpha = alpha_init  
	f_x = f(x)  
	grad_dot_d = np.dot(grad_f(x), d) # \nabla f(x)^Td  
	
	# Armijo cond: f(x + α*d) \leqd f(x) + c*α* \nabla f(x)^Td  
	while f(x + alpha * d) > f_x + c * alpha * grad_dot_d:  
		alpha *= rho # backtrace
		 
	return alpha
 
def conjugate_gradient(
    f: Callable[[np.ndarray], float],
    grad_f: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray],
    x0: np.ndarray,
    max_iter: int = 1000,
    tol: float = 1e-6
) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, float, int]:
	x = x0.copy()
	n = len(x)
	
	g = grad_f(x)
	d = -g.copy()
	
	iterations = 0
	
	for i in range(max_iter):
		if np.linalg.norm(g) < tol:
			break
		
		alpha = backtracking_line_search(f, grad_f, x, d)
		x_new = x + alpha * d
		g_new = grad_f(x_new)
		beta = np.dot(g_new, g_new) / np.dot(g, g)
		d = -g_new + beta * d
		x = x_new
		g = g_new
		
		iterations += 1
		
		# reset direction
		if (i + 1) % n == 0:
			d = -g.copy()
		
	return x, f(x), iterations

def steepest_descent(

    grad_f: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray],
    x0: np.ndarray,
    alpha: float = 0.01,  # fixed or line search
    max_iter: int = 1000,
    tol: float = 1e-6

    x = x0.copy()

        x = x - alpha * g
        iterations += 1
        
    return x, f(x), iterations

A arrow(c) = arrow(b)
Or we can use

where P is the selected polynomial. Then
c_j = ((f, P_j)_w)/((P_j, P_j)_w) = (integral_(-1)^1 w(x) f(x) P_j (x) d x)/(integral_(-1)^1 w(x) P_j^2 (x) d x) = (integral_(-1)^1 w(x) f(x) P_j (x) d x)/(||P_j ||^2)
where (f, P_j)_w is weighted inner-product.

where
q(x) = (x - x_1)(x - x_2) ...(x - x_n)
Crude Error

where h = max_i Delta t_i and M is constant with |f^((n)) | <= M.

import numpy as np
 
def T(j, x):
    """Compute Chebyshev polynomial T_j(x) = cos(j * arccos(x))"""
    return np.cos(j * np.arccos(x))
 
def chebyshev_interp(f, n, t):
    """
    Use Chebyshev polynomials T_j(x) and Gauss-Chebyshev quadrature
    to interpolate function f on interval [-1, 1].
    
    f: function to interpolate
    n: number of basis functions
    t: array of evaluation points
    """
    # chebyshev_nodes
    x_nodes = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        x_nodes[i] = np.cos((2 * i + 1) * np.pi / (2 * n))
    
    f_vals = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        f_vals[i] = f(x_nodes[i])
    
    coeffs = np.empty(n)
    for j in range(n):
        num = 0
        denom = 0
        for i in range(n):
            Tij = T(j, x_nodes[i])
            num += f_vals[i] * Tij
            denom += Tij * Tij
        num *= np.pi / n
        denom *= np.pi / n
        coeffs[j] = num / denom
    
    res = np.empty_like(t)
    for i in range(len(t)):
        s = 0
        for j in range(n):
            s += coeffs[j] * T(j, t[i])
        res[i] = s
    
    return res
